    label_en: Coconut — continuous hidden-state feedback
    anchor: coconut-continuous-thought

### Coconut: feeding a hidden state back instead of choosing a word In a text chain of thought, the model produces a hidden state, maps it to vocabulary logits, selects a token, and looks up that token's embedding for the next position. Coconut changes the connection between successive positions: during a latent interval, the previous last-layer hidden state itself becomes the next input embedding. The next position still requires a model pass. It does not require choosing a vocabulary item. ![[00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/coconut-2026-10-29/coconut.png|Coconut: token embedding feedback compared with continuous hidden-state feedback]] *Shibo Hao et al., [Coconut, original repository diagram](https://github.com/facebookresearch/coconut/blob/27273cb8cca4bb763c041a63b036d0c3b7cbbb48/assets/coconut.png). The left panel feeds a selected word back through the embedding table. The right panel feeds a last-layer state directly into the next position between the two boundary markers. Complete original PNG; repository [MIT notice](/licenses/coconut-27273cb8-MIT.txt).* The paper uses `` and `` to mark the beginning and end of the latent interval. The released code names them `<|start-latent|>` and `<|end-latent|>`. Its `<|latent|>` token identifies a position whose ordinary embedding must be replaced. Feeding the unchanged embedding of that placeholder would instead implement repeated discrete pause tokens. Suppose the question and beginning marker produce the state $h_0$. The first latent position receives $u_1=h_0$. The Transformer processes this new position with causal attention to the existing prefix and produces $h_1$. The second latent position receives $u_2=h_1$. After the chosen number of latent positions, the end marker receives its ordinary token embedding and language generation resumes. Writing $F_\theta$ for the last-position output of the causal Transformer, the recurrence is $$ \begin{aligned} u_1&=h_0,\\ u_{j+1}&=F_\theta(Q,\mathrm{bot},u_1,\ldots,u_j). \end{aligned} $$ Here $Q$ denotes the question embeddings. Every latent vector has the same width as an input embedding; in the paper the returned hidden states have passed the model's final normalization. Positions and causal attention are still needed. A latent step is an extra sequence position, not an extra Transformer layer and not a modification of the prompt alone. The released [`Coconut.forward`](https://github.com/facebookresearch/coconut/blob/27273cb8cca4bb763c041a63b036d0c3b7cbbb48/coconut.py#L38-L185) replaces the embedding at each latent position with the preceding last-layer hidden state. It keeps an offset when earlier positions have already been processed through a KV cache. An off-by-one error would feed a different position's state into the recurrence. #### Learning the latent interval A normal pretrained model has not necessarily learned to use its final hidden states as future input embeddings. The original Coconut recipe therefore starts from examples with written reasoning and gradually removes early reasoning steps while adding latent positions. Weights change during this training. After training, inference can vary the latent budget without changing those weights. For three annotated reasoning steps $r_1,r_2,r_3$ and two latent positions per removed step, the schedule has the following form. Boundary markers are omitted from the table but remain in the actual input. | Training stage | Visible reasoning after the question | Latent positions before that text | |---|---|---| | 0 | $r_1,r_2,r_3$, answer | 0 | | 1 | $r_2,r_3$, answer | 2 | | 2 | $r_3$, answer | 4 | | 3 | answer | 6 | A reasoning step is an annotated piece of text and can contain several tokens. Replacing one step with two vectors is not the same as replacing two tokens with two vectors. The parameter $c$ specifies latent positions per removed step; the remaining text still uses the model's tokenizer. In [`get_cot_latent_dataset`](https://github.com/facebookresearch/coconut/blob/27273cb8cca4bb763c041a63b036d0c3b7cbbb48/dataset.py#L232-L325), the question, latent positions and both boundary markers receive label `-100`. The surviving reasoning suffix, answer and EOS retain their token targets. The causal LM loss compares each target with the logits at the preceding position. Ignoring a target does not remove that position from the context. For example, after stage 1 the input contains the question, the start marker, two latent positions, the end marker, $r_2$, $r_3$ and the answer. The model is supervised on $r_2$, $r_3$ and the answer, including EOS. It is not given a target vector for either latent position and is not required to reconstruct the removed sentence $r_1$. Later token losses train the hidden-state recurrence through back-propagation. The paper resets optimizer state between curriculum stages. The pinned `run.py` reconstructs AdamW at **every epoch** when `reset_optimizer` is enabled, even if several epochs share one stage. Reproducing this revision requires keeping that distinction; the prose schedule alone does not specify the complete training run. #### A worked feedback calculation The following small calculation isolates the feedback connection. It is a two-dimensional linear recurrence, not a Transformer and not a trained reasoning model. Let the initial state be $(0.75,0.25)$ and let $$ A(a)= \begin{pmatrix} a&1\\ 1&-a \end{pmatrix}. $$ At $a=1$, direct state feedback gives $(1,0.5)$ after the first update and $(1.5,0.5)$ after the second. Now introduce two discrete tokens with embeddings $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ and choose the larger state coordinate as the next token. That discrete path selects the first token, processes $(1,0)$ and obtains $(1,1)$. With a fixed first-token tie break it obtains $(1,1)$ again. The continuous and discrete paths already differ before any claim about task quality. A toy two-class readout of the final coordinates gives probability $\operatorname{sigmoid}(1)\approx0.7311$ to the first class on the latent path and 0.5 on the discrete path. Neither probability is an accuracy. They show how selecting a vocabulary item changes the state passed onward. The code also checks the training gradient. For two continuous updates, the logit difference is $(a^2+1)/2$. The derivative of the first-class negative log-likelihood at $a=1$ is therefore $\operatorname{sigmoid}(1)-1$. Freezing the first state while differentiating the second update gives a different derivative. This models the error introduced by detaching a latent state during training. ```python import math def coconut_linear_step(state, a): x, y = state return (a * x + y, x - a * y) def coconut_toy_loss(a, freeze_first=False): h0 = (0.75, 0.25) h1 = coconut_linear_step(h0, 1.0 if freeze_first else a) h2 = coconut_linear_step(h1, a) return math.log1p(math.exp(h2[1] - h2[0])) def coconut_stage(question, steps, answer, stage, thoughts_per_step=2): if type(stage) is not int or not 0 <= stage <= len(steps): raise ValueError("stage must select a prefix of reasoning steps") if type(thoughts_per_step) is not int or thoughts_per_step < 1: raise ValueError("thoughts_per_step must be a positive integer") prefix = (list(question) + [""] + [""] * (stage * thoughts_per_step) + [""]) suffix = [token for step in steps[stage:] for token in step] suffix += list(answer) + [""] return prefix + suffix, [-100] * len(prefix) + suffix h0 = (0.75, 0.25) h1 = coconut_linear_step(h0, 1.0) h2 = coconut_linear_step(h1, 1.0) assert h1 == (1.0, 0.5) and h2 == (1.5, 0.5) hard_state = h0 for _ in range(2): embedding = (1.0, 0.0) if hard_state[0] >= hard_state[1] else (0.0, 1.0) hard_state = coconut_linear_step(embedding, 1.0) assert hard_state == (1.0, 1.0) eps = 1e-6 gradient = (coconut_toy_loss(1 + eps) - coconut_toy_loss(1 - eps)) / (2 * eps) detached = (coconut_toy_loss(1 + eps, True) - coconut_toy_loss(1 - eps, True)) / (2 * eps) expected = 1 / (1 + math.exp(-1)) - 1 assert math.isclose(gradient, expected, abs_tol=1e-9) assert math.isclose(detached, 1.5 * expected, abs_tol=1e-9) tokens, labels = coconut_stage(["Q"], [["r1a", "r1b"], ["r2"], ["r3"]], ["A"], stage=1) assert tokens == ["Q", "", "", "", "", "r2", "r3", "A", ""] assert labels == [-100] * 5 + ["r2", "r3", "A", ""] ``` The packing function demonstrates the stated curriculum and label boundary. It deliberately leaves out the source implementation's stage randomization, maximum-stage padding and distributed batching. It is not a replacement for the released training data pipeline. #### Latent steps still cost computation With $n$ latent positions, the released forward method makes $n+1$ backbone calls: one call for the prefix, sequential calls needed to form the latent inputs, and a final call for the surviving language suffix. KV caching can avoid recomputing an unchanged prefix; it does not make the dependent latent updates parallel. The reference backbone also computes vocabulary logits at intermediate positions even when they are not used to select tokens. The pinned `generate` supports batch size 1. After its initial latent forward pass, the text-generation loop passes the complete accumulated embedding sequence to the backbone again, rather than maintaining a serving engine's incremental text KV cache. Timing that implementation against optimized autoregressive serving would conflate the reasoning method with implementation choices. The original study uses a fixed latent length for most reported inference, rather than interpreting every hidden state as an automatically chosen stopping decision. More latent positions can be tested on the same trained weights, but a budget outside the training distribution is not guaranteed to improve the answer. The paper's tree-search interpretation comes from probing possible next concepts on ProsQA. The released forward loop contains no explicit BFS queue, exhaustive branch expansion or completeness guarantee. A state can support several alternative continuations without being a list of independently verified paths. This differs from the explicit frontier maintained by Tree of Thoughts above. Results also depend on the task. In [Table 1 of the pinned paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06769v3#S5), Coconut improves on text CoT on ProsQA but is below it on GSM8K; a pause-token curriculum is a strong control on ProsQA. Those experiments do not establish that hidden-state feedback is universally more accurate, or that printing fewer words always uses fewer FLOPs.
